The actual construction of the machine proves that the design on which it was based undoubtedly contained something true. It also proves that the “counter-design” which claimed that such a machine could not be built was false.
Exactly the same is true of a successful revolution.
Its success definitively reveals the falsehood in that part of the pre-revolutionary ideology which opposed the revolutionary idea.
And the success of the revolution also allows us to separate truth from error within the revolutionary idea itself.
Every revolutionary claim that dies in the course of revolutionary struggle must be regarded as a false opinion—as mere “revolutionary ideology.”
What remains of the revolutionary idea in the ideology adopted by the post-revolutionary state is what we possess as definitive, though partial, knowledge.
Within that ideology, whatever has undergone dialectical testing by becoming the object of revolutionary struggle can be regarded as definitive knowledge.
But because this knowledge is only partial, it cannot make up the whole content of the new post-revolutionary ideology.

The philosopher must therefore once again question everything that lies beyond the limits of what has actually been tested. He must await the appearance of a new revolutionary ideology and a new revolutionary struggle. That struggle will test another aspect of the existing ideology and, in doing so, supply another fragment of genuine knowledge about humanity and its world.
And so the process continues—but not forever.
The study of historical dialectic shows that this process has an endpoint.
At the level of humanity as a whole, revolutionary struggle ultimately creates a classless communist society in which all social and political contradictions have been eliminated.
This will therefore be the final society.

It will no longer contain mutually opposed ideologies, and the philosopher will no longer have to choose between them. The claims accepted by this society will no longer be ideology but genuine knowledge.

Why? Because this society will be the final result of all the revolutionary struggles humanity has undergone, and it will preserve within itself only what has survived the testing of dialectical struggle.

We can therefore say that the knowledge possessed by this society will be total knowledge: the knowledge of everything. The human being who belongs to it will cease to change because, within that society, humanity will have realized all its possibilities for life.
The philosopher who belongs to communist society will therefore be able to possess total knowledge.
In other words, he will be a sage.

Already today, then, our knowledge that historical dialectic exists, and our understanding of its character, allow us to say with certainty that “wisdom” is in principle attainable. There is therefore nothing irrational about trying to reach it—in other words, about being a philosopher.

But historical dialectic, and our knowledge of it, does more than give us this “faith,” this confident hope directed toward the future. It also gives us, here and now, knowledge that is partial but nevertheless absolutely true. As such, this knowledge already forms part of the future “wisdom.”
In other words, dialectic already gives us philosophical knowledge.
As I said earlier, Hegel was the first to discover clearly this real dialectic at work in work and struggle.
We can now see that Hegelian dialectic plays exactly the role that dialectic was supposed to play for Descartes and Plato.
On the one hand, it teaches the philosopher to question everything that anyone—including the philosopher himself—takes to be true knowledge.

On the other hand, it enables him to answer some of the questions he has raised. It lets him extract from the general mass of “opinions” certain fragments of “knowledge,” whether genuinely true or consciously recognized as false.
But there is an essential difference between Hegel’s dialectic and that of Plato and Descartes.
Hegel succeeds precisely where his predecessors failed.
Before Hegel, philosophers believed that the philosopher himself created the dialectic. The process was supposed to arise not from reality itself but from human thought about reality.
In other words, dialectic was regarded as a phenomenon of pure discourse, or logic. It was thought to require no real, physical effort on the part of human beings.
Hegel understood that things are actually very different.
The philosopher does not create the dialectic. He simply observes and describes it.
The dialectic exists outside him. It is present in reality itself, in the natural and historical world to which the philosopher himself belongs.
It is true that knowledge—truth—arises through the confrontation of opinions. But this “confrontation” is by no means merely verbal.
Opinions clash both in physical work and in bloody struggle.
Only this dialectical testing through work and struggle can finally separate truth from falsehood.

The philosopher can therefore move toward his ideal of total knowledge only by taking account of this real, historical dialectic and treating its description as an indispensable part of philosophy: its “dialectical” or “interrogative” part, the first part that introduces us to philosophy as a whole.

In Hegel’s own work, this first, dialectical part of philosophy is called a Phenomenology. I will keep that name out of respect for this great thinker, who was also the teacher of Marx, Lenin, and Stalin.
Even so, there remains an essential difference between Hegel’s view and that of Marxism-Leninism-Stalinism.
Because Hegel believed that he was living at the “end of time,” he could also believe himself capable of presenting a complete, “encyclopedic” system of true knowledge.
From his point of view, the second, “systematic” or “dogmatic” part of his philosophy was therefore no longer philosophy—the love or pursuit of wisdom—but Sophia itself: wisdom.
The first, dialectical part—the Phenomenology—then appeared as the introduction or path leading to wisdom, and thus as what we would ordinarily call “philosophy.”
Hegel’s System can therefore be divided into Phenomenology, or philosophy, on the one hand, and wisdom, or knowledge—what Hegel himself calls Science—on the other.
The second part of the System contains perfect knowledge: total knowledge.
In principle, it says everything that can be said about nature and humanity.
At first sight, then, it might seem that this second part should be enough on its own.
The “Sage” must genuinely know everything. This means knowing not only what can be known about natural and human reality but also how it can be known.
He must know the content of knowledge, but he must also know knowledge itself.
And it is the Phenomenology that gives him this knowledge of knowledge.
Phenomenology describes the real, historical dialectic of work and struggle. It shows how humanity eventually arrived at total knowledge, or wisdom.

It therefore shows that the knowledge presented in the second part really is total knowledge: first, that it is genuinely knowledge rather than opinion, and second, that it is knowledge of everything.
From the standpoint of Marxism-Leninism-Stalinism, however, there can be no question of attaining complete and final knowledge today.
Such knowledge is possible only in communist society, and communist society has not yet been fully realized.
Until it is, only partial knowledge is possible, and for the time being every attempt to complete that knowledge must be treated as open to question.
The second, “dogmatic” part of a Marxist “system” therefore cannot be identified with wisdom. It remains a philosophy.
A Marxist Phenomenology is consequently only an introduction to this philosophy.

This also means that our Phenomenology can describe historical dialectic only partially and incompletely, just as the philosophical knowledge to be presented in the second part of the “system” must itself remain partial and incomplete. Phenomenology is merely the introduction and the path leading to that second part.
A phenomenological introduction to philosophy can, in principle, gather together and unite all the true knowledge about the world and humanity that is available to us at a given historical moment.
But the same introduction also shows that this knowledge is partial.
Philosophy, however, necessarily aims at complete knowledge, because it finds the criterion of its truth only in the circularity of the knowledge it presents.
It must therefore supplement partial knowledge with certain “hypotheses” or “opinions”—or, if one prefers, with certain “ideologies.”

At the same time, it must remain aware that the future development of the real, historical dialectical process may force it to revise its “systematic” part in response to changes in its phenomenological part—the part in which this continuing and expanding dialectic must be described.
We naturally do not know what will happen to our system in the future.
But we do know what happened to Hegel’s.
His supposed “wisdom” turned out, in the end, to be the ideology of the revolutionary bourgeoisie of the early nineteenth century.
The proletarian revolution that has emerged in our own time has therefore demonstrated the need for a fundamental revision of his system.

To make this revision, we must first expand his Phenomenology by describing dialectical stages Hegel himself did not know: stages represented by the proletarian ideology formulated by Marx, the revolutionary idea of Lenin, and Stalin’s definitive realization of the revolution.
In other words, it is not enough to produce a new, revised and corrected edition of the “systematic” or “dogmatic” part of Hegelian philosophy, necessary though that revision has become.
It must also be preceded by a revised and corrected edition of its introductory—that is, its “phenomenological” or “dialectical”—part.
The book presented here is nothing other than such a revised and corrected edition of Hegel’s Phenomenology, interpreted in the light of Marxism-Leninism-Stalinism.

Before we describe historical dialectic in the main body of the Phenomenology, however, we must explain in greater detail what Phenomenology is when understood as an introduction to philosophy: as a path toward partial knowledge which nevertheless claims to provide a firm foundation for the system of perfect knowledge that the future human being of communist society will create.
Phenomenology as a dialectical introduction to philosophy
The best answer to the question “What is a dialectical introduction to philosophy?”—what, following Hegel, I call a Phenomenology—is the book in which that Phenomenology is actually presented.
Once readers have finished it, they will have a clear and complete understanding of its purpose, its subject, and the means—its method—by which that subject is treated and its purpose achieved.
They will also understand its structure: the order in which the subject must be treated, using the appropriate method, if the stated purpose is to be achieved.
In a certain sense, we can go further. Reading the book as a whole is not merely the best answer to questions about it. It is the only possible and convincing answer.
Here too, a kind of “technical” test is unavoidable.

Only if the “project” is actually carried out—only if the book is written, read, and recognized as successful—can we finally be convinced that what the introduction says about the book, before it has in a sense been constructed, was correct.
Only the recognized success of the book can genuinely convince us that the purpose it set itself was legitimate and that it chose a subject appropriate to that purpose.
Only the success of the book can prove that its method was well chosen and thereby justify that method.

And only the finished book can give a convincing explanation of its structure: it alone can show why, given its purpose and method, the subject had to be treated in this particular order rather than another.
Still, a book whose contents are varied, complex, and at times difficult is easier to read if a few preliminary remarks are made about its purpose, subject, method, and structure.
This is especially true of a Phenomenology.
First, unlike most other sciences, the purpose of a Phenomenology does not simply coincide with its subject matter.
Usually, the purpose of a science is simply to study its own particular subject.

The subject of zoology, for example, is the animal world, and its purpose is to study that world. If the science of electricity aims to study electricity, then electricity is both its subject and its object.
Phenomenology is different because its purpose is not exhausted by the study of its object.
In this respect it can be compared with medicine. Medicine takes disease as its subject but health as its goal.
Something similar is true of Phenomenology.
It studies ideology and error, but its goal is to discover knowledge and truth.
In any case, the relation between the purpose of Phenomenology and the subject it studies is not immediately obvious. To understand Phenomenology properly, we therefore need to clarify that relation.
